newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries end lackluster week on positive note.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries end lackluster week on positive note.

text.p: Cheered by tame housing data and reports of central bank buying, prices of Treasury securities erased early losses to close substantially higher Friday.
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond closed up 14/32 at 99-05/32. The yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 6.82 percent from 6.85 percent Thursday.
The 5.875 percent two-year note ended up 2/32 at 99-30/32 to yield 5.91 percent.
The about-face occured after the Commerce Department reported that orders for durable goods, jumped a sharp 4.6 percent in September.

The strong headline number prompted a sharp drop in the Treasury market. But after a closer look at the report, the market regained its footing, seizing on a 17.5 percent surge in transportation equipment orders, which accounted for a majority of the overall rise.
Economists said a recent string of aircraft and parts orders from Boeing Co. appeared to have been lumped into the September figures, boosting the transportation sector's contribution to the report.
Excluding transportation, orders rose by a more modest and market-friendly 0.9 percent.
"If you take a look at the total, excluding transportation, durable goods really did not increase all that much," said Samuel Kahan, president of ASK Financial Research Ltd.
As traders re-evaluated the durables report, prices were given an extra boost by reports of central bank buying in the short-to-intermediate sector of the yield curve.
"I heard the Fed was in and I also heard of foreign central banks outright buying in the market," said John Spinello, government bond strategist at Merrill Lynch Government Securities Inc.
Reports that the Federal Reserve has been active in buying securities under the table have provided a modicum of support to a lethargic market throughout the week.
Lending further support to the market was the National Association of Realtors' (NAR) report on September existing home sales.
The NAR said that sales of existing homes fell by a surprisingly hefty 2.9 percent in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.02 million units from a revised 4.14 million units in August.
"The drop in home sales was bigger than expected and the market liked that," said Suzanne Rizzo, U.S. economist at financial adivsory firm MFR Inc.

NAR President Art Godi said the September sales figures reflected consumer caution in the wake of higher interest rates. However, the group's chief economist, John Tuccillo, said mortgage rates have likely peaked for the year.
Overshadowed by the good news in the home sales report was the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index, which rose from already strong levels.

The final sentiment index for October posted a solid rise to 96.5 vs. 94.7 in September. The current conditions component of the report also posted a strong gain, while the expectations index fell slightly to 89.9 from 90.1 in September.
The market has ignored strong consumer confidence numbers of late because they have yet to translate into gains in consumer spending.
Investors in the investment grade corporate bond market continued to focus on the cable sector, as prices in the overall market remained steady.

Spreads on Viacom Inc. 20-year bonds tightened by around 15 basis points after the company announced late in the day that it was dropping its settlement talks with Seagram Co. Ltd.'s MCA Inc. in a dispute over their jointly owned cable netowrk.

Prices on TCI Communications Inc. bonds continued to decline following the release earlier this week of poorer-than-expected earnings. "The company has lost a lot of credibility with the investment community," said one trader.
High-yield bond prices were generally flat, although traders said bonds in the casino and supermarket sector experienced some price weakness.

Trump Hotel & Casino Resorts 11 1/4 percent first mortgage notes due 2006 closed with a 95 1/2 bid, after trading as low as 94 earlier in the day. Casino America 12 1/2 senior secured notes of 2003 closed at 102 1/2 after trading as low as 101 1/2, traders said.
On a more positive note for bond holders, Hilton Hotels Corp. made a cash offer to purchase roughly $1 billion in debt of Bally's Grand Inc. at a premium to where the bonds were trading.

"Bonds were expecting a higher tender price, but fundamentally it's still a positive because they will tender for them at a premium," said one trader. He speculated that the bond holders may negotiate for an even higher price at a later date.
U.S. municipal bonds ended unchanged to 1/4 point higher, buoyed by stronger Treasuries, but next week will see another flood of new issues, estimated at $5.175 billion, which could hit prices.
A total of around $4.8 billion of bonds were sold this week, with most deals doing surprisingly well.
"I don't think they gave up as much yield this week at they thought they would have to," a trader said.
